power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Purpose: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains refractory to immunotherapy due to its immunosuppressive microenvironment.
Tumour-infiltrating cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells express elevated programmed cell death protein-1 (PD-1), suggesting checkpoint-mediated dysfunction may limit T-cell therapy.
We evaluated the safety and immunological activity of allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) combined with pembrolizumab.
In this phase I 3+3 dose-escalation study, recurrent GBM patients received four weekly infusions of CYT-101 followed by pembrolizumab.
The primary endpoint was safety.
Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival at 6 months (PFS-6), overall survival at 6 months (OS-6), and immune correlates of response.
Results: CYT-101 T-cell therapy demonstrated polyfunctional activity, broad HLA restriction, potent cytolytic function, and diverse T-cell receptor repertoires.
Nine patients received study treatment.
No dose-limiting toxicities were observed, and the maximum tolerated dose was not reached.
Only six adverse events were considered treatment-related, and no treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity occurred.
OS-6 and PFS-6 were 55% and 11%, respectively, with a median overall survival of 9.1 months.
No objective clinical responses were seen.
Of the nine treated participants, one had stable disease, five had progressive disease, and three were unevaluable by modified RANO criteria.

Immune profiling revealed enhanced global CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell function following CYT-101 therapy, while donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected in six of nine participants, with significant T-cell repertoire remodelling.
Conclusions: Allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy combined with pembrolizumab was safe in recurrent GBM, supporting further evaluation of this strategy to overcome immune dysfunction in GBM.
Glioblastoma (GBM) remains a major therapeutic challenge, with limited benefit from immune checkpoint blockade or adoptive cellular therapies when used independently.

This phase I study provides clinical evidence that combining an off-the-shelf, allogeneic cytomegalovirus (CMV)specific T-cell therapy (CYT-101) with PD-1 blockade is safe, feasible, and immunologically active in recurrent GBM.
CYT-101 demonstrated a favourable safety profile without graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, or treatment-related serious adverse events.

Importantly, donor-derived CYT-101 clonotypes were detected following infusion, accompanied by enhanced systemic CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell function and substantial T-cell repertoire remodelling following CYT-101 and pembrolizumab.

These findings provide proof-of-concept that allogeneic virus-specific T cells can be safely combined with checkpoint inhibition in GBM, supporting further clinical development and evaluation in larger studies.
Clinical studies of pembrolizumab in recurrent GBM following standard chemoradiotherapy have failed to demonstrate a significant survival benefit (9).
Adoptive cellular immunotherapy using cytomegalovirus (CMV)-specific T cells has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach for GBM (10, 11).

text.text: Multiple studies have reported the expression of CMV antigens within malignant glioma cells, providing a rationale for targeting CMV-associated epitopes in GBM (12-14).
Several approaches have been assessed targeting CMV in GBM.
These include pp65 mRNA-loaded dendritic cell vaccines and CMV peptide vaccines, and antiviral therapy with valganciclovir (13,15-21).
In our previous clinical studies, adoptively transferred CMV-specific T cells trafficked to tumour sites and mediated anti-tumour immune responses (22, 23).

text.text: However, detailed immune profiling revealed that tumour-infiltrating CMVspecific T cells expressed elevated levels of inhibitory checkpoint molecules, including PD-1, compared with their circulating counterparts (23).
These findings suggested that transferred CMV-specific T cells may become functionally restrained within the tumour microenvironment through PD-1-mediated immune suppression.

Preclinical and clinical studies across multiple tumour types have demonstrated that immune checkpoint blockade can enhance the expansion, persistence, and effector function of adoptively transferred T cells, supporting a synergistic interaction between adoptive cellular therapy and PD-1 inhibition (24, 25).

text.text: Programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) is an inhibitory immune checkpoint receptor expressed on activated T cells.

Engagement of PD-1 by its ligands, programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and programmed death-ligand 2 (PD-L2), suppresses T-cell activation and effector function, thereby maintaining peripheral immune tolerance (7, 8).

text.text: Many cancers exploit this pathway to evade immune surveillance, making PD-1 blockade an attractive therapeutic strategy.
Pembrolizumab is a humanised immunoglobulin G4 monoclonal antibody that binds PD-1 and prevents its interaction with PD-L1 and PD-L2.

In contrast, participants NEW-03, NEW-06, and NEW-12 demonstrated peak frequencies of donor-derived clonotypes after pembrolizumab initiation, suggesting that PD-1 blockade may have contributed to the persistence or expansion of transferred T-cell populations in a subset of patients.

text.text: Although the magnitude of expansion was generally lower than that observed following CYT-101 therapy, substantial repertoire remodelling was evident, particularly in participants NEW-09 (n = 152 expanded clonotypes) and NEW-03 (n = 148 expanded clonotypes).
Three of the four participants who failed to demonstrate significant repertoire changes following pembrolizumab (NEW-07, NEW-11, and NEW-12) experienced relatively poor overall survival.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CYT-101 adoptive immunotherapy induces measurable peripheral T-cell expansion and repertoire remodelling, while subsequent PD-1 blockade is associated with additional clonal dynamics in a subset of patients.
The relationship between these immunological changes and clinical outcome warrants further investigation in larger studies.
GBM remains one of the most challenging malignancies to treat, with limited therapeutic advances despite substantial efforts to harness the immune system (28, 29).
text.formatted: GBM remains one of the most challenging malignancies to treat, with limited therapeutic advances despite substantial efforts to harness the immune system <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29)</ref>.

text.text: In this phase I study, we evaluated the safety and biological activity of CYT-101, an allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy, administered in combination with pembrolizumab in patients with recurrent GBM.

The combination was well tolerated, with no dose-limiting toxicities, treatment-related serious adverse events, graft-versus-host disease, cytokine release syndrome, or neurotoxicity observed at any dose level.

Importantly, longitudinal immune monitoring demonstrated evidence of allogeneic donor-derived T-cell persistence and treatment-associated remodelling of the peripheral T-cell repertoire, supporting the immunological activity of this combination approach.

Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed the treatment of several solid tumours; however, clinical trials of anti-PD-1 therapy in GBM have failed to demonstrate meaningful improvements in survival (30) (31) (32).
text.formatted: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed the treatment of several solid tumours; however, clinical trials of anti-PD-1 therapy in GBM have failed to demonstrate meaningful improvements in survival <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(32)</ref>.

text.text: One explanation for this lack of efficacy is the profoundly immunosuppressive and immunologically "cold" nature of the GBM microenvironment, which is characterised by limited T-cell infiltration, extensive myeloid-mediated immune suppression, Tcell dysfunction, and multiple mechanisms of immune evasion (33, 34).

text.text: Checkpoint blockade alone may therefore be insufficient in the absence of a pre-existing tumour-reactive T-cell population (35, 36).
text.formatted: Checkpoint blockade alone may therefore be insufficient in the absence of a pre-existing tumour-reactive T-cell population <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36)</ref>.

text.text: We previously demonstrated that tumour-infiltrating CMV-specific T cells express elevated levels of PD-1 following adoptive transfer, suggesting that transferred T cells may become susceptible to checkpoint-mediated inhibition within the tumour microenvironment (23).

text.text: The current study was designed to address this limitation by combining adoptive cellular therapy with PD-1 blockade.
The favourable safety profile observed supports further clinical evaluation of this strategy.
A notable feature of this study was the use of an allogeneic virus-specific T-cell product.
Unlike autologous approaches, allogeneic CYT-101 could be manufactured in advance, cryopreserved, and administered without delay.
This approach overcomes many logistical barriers associated with individualised cell therapies, including manufacturing failures, variable product quality, and prolonged vein-to-vein times.
Importantly, no evidence of graft-versus-host disease was observed, despite repeated infusions of partially HLA-matched donor T cells.

These findings are consistent with our previous studies demonstrating the safety of virus-specific T-cell therapies in patients with cancer and transplant recipients (22, (37) (38) (39) (40) and support the feasibility of developing off-the-shelf cellular immunotherapies for patients with GBM.
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with our previous studies demonstrating the safety of virus-specific T-cell therapies in patients with cancer and transplant recipients <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(37)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(38)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(39)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(40)</ref> and support the feasibility of developing off-the-shelf cellular immunotherapies for patients with GBM.

text.text: Although this study was not designed to evaluate efficacy, several observations suggest that CYT-101 induced measurable immunological activity.
Following therapy, we observed enhanced global CD4 + and CD8 + T-cell function, as demonstrated by increased IFN-γ production after polyclonal stimulation.
Interestingly, these changes occurred in the absence of consistent expansion of circulating CMV-specific T cells.
This finding suggests that the immunological effects of CYT-101 may extend beyond simple expansion of virus-specific populations and may involve broader activation of endogenous immune responses.
Similar phenomena have been observed in other cellular therapy settings, where adoptively transferred T cells promote epitope spreading and secondary immune activation (22, 41, 42).
text.formatted: Similar phenomena have been observed in other cellular therapy settings, where adoptively transferred T cells promote epitope spreading and secondary immune activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42)</ref>.

text.text: One of the most important findings of this study was the detection of donor-derived CYT-101 TCR clonotypes in six of nine participants following treatment.
These data provide direct evidence that transferred allogeneic T cells can persist in vivo following infusion.

The ability to track infused clonotypes using single-cell TCR sequencing and bulk repertoire analysis has emerged as an important tool for understanding the fate of adoptively transferred cells and their contribution to therapeutic responses (43, 44).
text.formatted: The ability to track infused clonotypes using single-cell TCR sequencing and bulk repertoire analysis has emerged as an important tool for understanding the fate of adoptively transferred cells and their contribution to therapeutic responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44)</ref>.

text.text: While donor-derived clonotypes generally contracted over time, a subset of patients demonstrated peak frequencies following the commencement of pembrolizumab, raising the possibility that PD-1 blockade may enhance the persistence or expansion of transferred T cells.
Previous preclinical and clinical studies have shown that checkpoint blockade can improve the survival, expansion, and functional capacity of adoptively transferred T cells (45, 46).
text.formatted: Previous preclinical and clinical studies have shown that checkpoint blockade can improve the survival, expansion, and functional capacity of adoptively transferred T cells <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46)</ref>.

text.text: Although this observation requires validation in larger studies, it provides preliminary support for the biological rationale underpinning this combination strategy.
Deep TCR repertoire sequencing further revealed substantial remodelling of the peripheral T-cell compartment following treatment.
All participants exhibited significant clonal expansion after CYT-101 administration, while a distinct wave of repertoire changes emerged following pembrolizumab treatment in a subset of patients.
These findings suggest that the two therapies may exert complementary immunological effects.
CYT-101 appeared to drive an initial burst of T-cell expansion, whereas pembrolizumab was associated with subsequent diversification and remodelling of the T-cell repertoire.
Similar treatment-associated repertoire changes have been associated with clinical responses to adoptive cellular therapies and immune checkpoint blockade in other cancers (47, 48).
text.formatted: Similar treatment-associated repertoire changes have been associated with clinical responses to adoptive cellular therapies and immune checkpoint blockade in other cancers <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, the participants demonstrating the most pronounced repertoire dynamics included those with prolonged survival, suggesting that treatment-induced immune remodelling may represent a biomarker of therapeutic activity.
However, the small sample size precludes definitive conclusions regarding associations between repertoire changes and clinical outcomes.
The findings of this phase I study should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
As a phase I dose-escalation trial, the primary objective was safety rather than efficacy, and the small cohort size limited statistical power for clinical and correlative analyses.

Furthermore, the contribution of CYT-101 cannot be separated from the effect of pembrolizumab, and immune monitoring was performed primarily in peripheral blood, which may not fully capture immune dynamics occurring within the tumour microenvironment.
Future clinical studies using this treatment strategy should include a cohort of participants receiving CYT-101 alone, in addition to a cohort receiving the combined therapy.

Future studies incorporating paired tumour biopsies, cerebrospinal fluid analyses, and spatial immune profiling will be important to determine whether donor-derived T cells traffic to tumour sites and mediate local immune remodelling.

In addition, although CMV-associated antigens have been reported in GBM (49) (50) (51), the extent and biological significance of CMV expression in gliomas remains an area of ongoing investigation (13, 19, 52, 53).

text.text: In conclusion, this study demonstrates that allogeneic CMV-specific T-cell therapy can be safely combined with PD-1 blockade in patients with recurrent GBM.

The detection of donorderived clonotypes, enhancement of T-cell function, and extensive treatment-associated remodelling of the T-cell repertoire provide evidence of immunological activity and support further evaluation of this approach.
